title: Limitations of the Legacy Date and Calendar Classes

blocks.text: 7.3.1. Limitations of the Legacy Date and Calendar Classes

A booking service written before Java 8 gets three tickets in one week. Monday's standup moved from 08:00 to 07:45 UTC, and nobody asked for it. A guest booked a room for 30 February and was charged for 2 March. The nightly report puts a booking made at 23:30 UTC on Sunday on one server and on Monday on another. Each comes from how `java.util.Date`, `Calendar` or `SimpleDateFormat` behave by default.
Every output below comes from Java 21. Each run sets the default zone and locale explicitly: `-Duser.timezone=Europe/Amsterdam` unless stated, and `-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US`.
A Date Is a Mutable Moment, So Anyone Holding It Can Move It

A `Date` holds one `long`, milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00Z, and `setTime` changes it. The meeting keeps its start in a `private final Date` field and returns it from a getter. The reminder service wants a time 15 minutes earlier:
meeting starts: 2026-03-16T07:45:00Z

`final` fixes which object the field points to, not what is inside it. The getter handed out the meeting's own object, so the reminder service moved the meeting itself. The constructor stores the caller's object too, so a caller that reuses its `Date` for the next booking moves this meeting.

Where you must keep `Date`, copy it in the constructor and in the getter: `new Date(d.getTime())`. The `java.time` value types are immutable, and their `plus...` methods return a new object (unit 7.3.2).
<!-- practice 1 -->
Months Count From 0, Years From 1900, and Out-of-Range Values Roll Over
`Calendar` numbers months 0 to 11, and the deprecated `Date` constructors also take the year minus

items: By default neither rejects an out-of-range value: the excess carries into the next field.

blocks.text:
new Date(2026, 3, 15):        3926-04-15
cal.set(2026, 3, 15):         2026-04-15
cal.set(2026, 12, 1):         2027-01-01
cal.set(2026, FEBRUARY, 30):  2026-03-02
strict getTime():             java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: MONTH: 1 -> 2
getYear() 126, getMonth() 2

The year 2026 passed to the constructor became 3926, month 3 is April, month 12 is January of the next year, and 30 February is 2 March. The conventions are those of C's `struct tm` (`tm_year` since 1900, `tm_mon` from 0). Only the non-lenient calendar refused, and only when it next computed its fields. The bug appears wherever values cross into or out of the legacy API: a column written from `getMonth()` and read as a calendar month is a month early on every row. `LocalDate.of` counts months from 1 and throws on 30 February.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Parsing Is Lenient by Default, and Strict Mode Still Ignores What Follows the Date
`SimpleDateFormat.parse` uses the same lenient calendar:

lenient 2026-02-30     -> 2026-03-02
lenient 2026-13-01     -> 2027-01-01
lenient 2026-03-15abc  -> 2026-03-15
strict  2026-02-30     -> java.text.ParseException: Unparseable date: "2026-02-30"
strict  2026-03-15abc  -> 2026-03-15
strict  2026-3-5       -> 2026-03-05
parse stopped at index 10 of 13

The lenient formatter is how the guest got 2 March. Strict mode rejects impossible fields, but `parse(String)` stops reading once it has a date and returns it; the `ParsePosition` shows it stopped at index 10 of 13. `MM` does not require two digits, so `2026-3-5` passes. `LocalDate.parse(text)` reads the whole text and validates the date (a pattern formatter needs `ResolverStyle.STRICT` for the same check, unit 7.3.2.4):
LocalDate.parse: Text '2026-02-30' could not be parsed: Invalid date 'FEBRUARY 30'
<!-- practice 3 -->
One SimpleDateFormat Shared by Threads Returns Wrong Dates

Legacy code often keeps one formatter in a `static final` field. Four threads each parse 10,000 dates (1,000 distinct ones, ten times over) through one shared instance and compare every result with the text they passed in (run with `-Duser.timezone=UTC`):

A `SimpleDateFormat` keeps a `Calendar` and a `DecimalFormat` in instance fields and uses them as scratch space on every parse, so concurrent parses overwrite each other's partial results. The counts vary between runs, but in each one most failures return a date, another thread's or a mix that nobody passed in, and nothing logs them; the exceptions are the few you would notice. The class is not synchronized, and its javadoc advises a formatter per thread; pre-Java 8 code used a `ThreadLocal`, a new instance per call, or a lock. `DateTimeFormatter` is immutable and safe to share (unit 7.3.2.4).
<!-- practice 5 -->
A Date Has No Zone; toString() Uses the JVM's Default
The same `Date` printed in two JVMs, one started with `-Duser.timezone=Europe/Amsterdam` and one with `-Duser.timezone=America/New_York`:

getTime():  1773617400000
toString(): Mon Mar 16 00:30:00 CET 2026

getTime():  1773617400000
toString(): Sun Mar 15 19:30:00 EDT 2026

Both JVMs hold the same `getTime()`. `toString()`, the deprecated `getDate()` and `getHours()`, and a `SimpleDateFormat` without `setTimeZone` all use the JVM's default zone. That is the nightly report: the code that cut bookings into days never named a zone, so each server used its own, and `java.util` has no date-only type to hold the result. To get a day, name the zone: `d.toInstant().atZone(zone).toLocalDate()` (zones in unit 7.3.2.5).
java.sql.Date Is a java.util.Date That Breaks Its Parent's Contract
JDBC's date-only type, `java.sql.Date`, extends `java.util.Date` and still holds milliseconds. Its `toString()` prints only the day:

2026-03-15 equals 2026-03-15: false
getTime(): 1773565200000 vs 1773529200000
toInstant(): java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
getHours(): java.lang.IllegalArgumentException
Instant.ofEpochMilli(getTime()): 2026-03-15T09:00:00Z
fromText as a moment, in UTC: 2026-03-14
fromText.toLocalDate():       2026-03-15

The constructor keeps the time of day and `equals` compares `getTime()`, so two values that print the same day aren't equal, and a `Set` of them keeps both. The subclass also throws from methods its parent declares: a method that takes a `java.util.Date`, calls `toInstant()` and is tested only with `java.util.Date` values fails on the first value from `ResultSet.getDate` (`java.sql.Timestamp` doesn't throw). For a moment, `Instant.ofEpochMilli(d.getTime())` works on both types. A `java.sql.Date` names a day, though: `valueOf` stored midnight in the default zone, 23:00Z the day before, so reading it as a moment in another zone gives the wrong day, and `toLocalDate()` gives the right one. Conversions are unit 7.3.3.
<!-- practice 4 -->
Summary

items: **A `Date` is mutable**: a getter or constructor that shares one lets any caller move your moment, and `final` doesn't stop it.
**Months count from 0, years from 1900, and `Calendar` rolls overflow** into the next field instead of rejecting it.
**`SimpleDateFormat` parses leniently by default**, and strict mode still ignores text after the date.
**A shared `SimpleDateFormat` returns wrong dates under concurrency**, most of them silently.
**A `Date` has no zone or day**: `toString()` and `Date`'s deprecated field getters use the JVM default.
**`java.sql.Date` breaks `java.util.Date`'s contract**: `toInstant()` throws, values that print the same day can differ, and its day comes from `toLocalDate()`.

**Legacy behaviour (Java 21, from runs or the javadoc):**

rows: out-of-range fields throw `IllegalArgumentException` when the time is computed
lenient by default; ignores text after the date even when strict
`GMT`: an unknown ID is not an error
accepted; the javadoc deprecates three-letter IDs as ambiguous

Challenges

items: A library you can't change returns `Date` from its getters and keeps a reference. Where in your code do you convert, and what do you lose if a caller still needs the library's object?
Rerun the shared-formatter test with one thread and with 32. What do the counts tell you about catching this bug in a test suite?
A table stores `Date.getMonth()` values in a column named `month`. How do you migrate its readers without a day on which both conventions are live?

blocks.text: Design Note: One Type for Every Question

`java.util.Date` answers one question, "which millisecond", but the 1.0 API also made it answer "which day" and "which hour" through methods that used the default zone. JDK 1.1 deprecated those methods and moved calendar work to `Calendar` and text to `DateFormat`, but kept every type mutable and lenient by default. `java.time` (JSR 310, Java 8) gives each question its own immutable type, so a moment and a day have different types. The cost is at the boundary: legacy APIs still take and return `Date`, and converting to a day or a local time there needs an explicit zone.
